name: SSC CPO
fullName: Staff Selection Commission – Sub-Inspector in Delhi Police and Central Armed Police Forces Examination
approxCandidates: Several lakh applicants per cycle (official 2026 figure not published at check time)
eligibility: Bachelor's degree; 20–25 years (with category relaxations); Delhi Police SI (Exe.) male candidates need an LMV driving licence; physical standards and PET apply

notification.summary: SSC CPO 2026 was notified on 10 Sep 2026 for ≈1,871 tentative SI posts in Delhi Police, CAPFs and CISF (some reports say 2,018), with a revised Paper 1 pattern (100 questions, 1 hour). Applications closed on 30 Sep 2026, the correction window runs 8–10 Oct 2026, and Paper 1 is reportedly proposed for 20–28 Nov 2026.

pattern.notes: Revised in the 2026 notification (as reported by multiple coaching sites): Paper 1 cut from 200 questions/200 marks/2 hours to 100 questions/100 marks/1 hour, with a 15-minute timer per section; −0.25 per wrong answer. Paper 2 (English) reportedly expanded. Selection: Paper 1 → PET/PST → Paper 2 → DME. Verify on ssc.gov.in.

trendAnalysis.summary: Analysis is based on the 2023–2025 papers (old 50-questions-per-section format); the topic mix is expected to carry over to the shorter 2026 format. Paper 1 is moderate, close to CGL Tier 1 in level: Quant is the toughest (algebra, geometry, trigonometry, mensuration and DI ≈ 45% of the section), Reasoning is scoring (analogy, classification, series, coding, puzzles and figures), GK is static-heavy with a noticeable share of polity, history and police/defence-related questions, and English has vocabulary, grammar-based error spotting/improvement, narration and voice, plus cloze and comprehension. Sectional timing from 2026 makes time management per section critical.

pyqBlueprint.method: Compiled from the commission's published question-paper/response-sheet format and from shift-wise memory-based papers and topic-wise analyses published by coaching sites (Testbook, Adda247, PW, Careers360 day-wise analyses) for the 2023–2025 cycles, cross-checked against the writer's own knowledge of SSC papers. Live web fetches during this round returned only summary pages (SSC barred public discussion of 2025 papers), so question-type detail relies mainly on prior knowledge of the papers; frequencies are approximate per-shift counts. Figure-based (non-verbal) archetypes are recorded but only text-renderable variants are used for generated questions.

archetypes.pattern: Word-pair analogy (A : B :: C : ?) built on a semantic relation – worker : tool, product : raw material, organ : function, instrument : quantity measured, young one : animal; distractors are words of the same category that do not share the relation.

Number-pair/triad analogy where the second term comes from an arithmetic rule on the first (n² ± k, n³ ± k, ×k ± c, digit operations); often framed with two example pairs and a note to operate on whole numbers without splitting digits; distractors satisfy the rule for only one pair or come from ±1 slips.
Letter-cluster analogy (ABCD : EFGH :: ? ) where each letter moves by a fixed or alternating +/− shift or is replaced by its opposite letter (A↔Z); distractors differ in exactly one letter.
Odd-one-out among four words/objects by category or property (three belong to one class, e.g. instruments, organs, rivers of one state); the trap is a surface feature shared by the odd item.
Odd number / number-pair / triad out of four where three follow one arithmetic rule (squares, primes, (a, b, c) with c = a×b − k, divisibility); the odd option breaks the rule by a small margin.
Odd letter-cluster out of four where three clusters have the same positional gaps (e.g. +2, +3 or opposite-letter pairs) and one breaks the gap pattern.
Number series with one missing/next term following a two-step rule (×k + c, alternating operations, differences forming squares/primes or their own series).

Letter or alphanumeric cluster series (e.g. three-letter groups with each position advancing by its own increment, possibly mixed with numbers); find the next cluster; distractors shift one position wrongly.
Word → letter code by a positional rule (each letter shifted by +k/−k, alternate shifts, reversal then shift, or opposite letters); decode the rule from one example and encode a new word.

Word → number code from alphabet positions (sum of positions, sum × k, sum of reverse positions, number of letters × k); apply the rule to a new word; distractors use forward instead of reverse positions.
Sentence coding: two or three short sentences coded as groups of code words; identify the code of a given word by finding the common word/code between statements.
Verbal chain / introduction ('pointing to a photo…') blood relation: trace 3–4 links and name the relation; traps are gender assumptions and the paternal/maternal side.
Coded blood relations: symbols (A + B, A × B, A − B …) stand for relations; decode an expression to find how two people are related, or which expression makes a given relation true.

Walking path of 3–5 legs with left/right turns; find the shortest distance and/or direction from the start (often a Pythagorean triple); or the final facing direction after a sequence of left/right/clockwise turns; traps are direction after a 'right turn' and adding instead of subtracting legs.
Two/three statements ('All/Some/No') with two conclusions; decide which follow, including 'Some … are not' and possibility-type conclusions; trap is reversing 'All A are B'.
Symbol substitution: '+' means '×', '−' means '÷' etc.; rewrite and evaluate an expression with BODMAS; distractors come from left-to-right evaluation.
Which two signs (or two numbers) must be interchanged to make a given equation correct; each option names a pair of signs to swap.
Missing term inside a number sequence (often the middle term) built from a mixed rule such as ×1 + 1, ×2 + 2, ×3 + 3 … or alternating × and +; find the term that replaces '?'.
Defined-operation missing number: from two or three solved examples (a ★ b = …) infer the rule (a² + b², (a + b)², a×b + a …) and apply it; distractors fit just one example.
Number grid / figure (given as rows): each row or column follows the same rule (e.g. third = first × second − k, or sum of squares); find the missing number.

Position from both ends: total in a row/class from two ranks, rank from the other end, persons between two people, or a short comparison chain (taller/older) to find who is at a rank; trap is ±1 counting.
Arrange 5 words in dictionary order (common prefix, differing late letters) or find which word comes at a given position.
Calendar: day of the week for a date given a reference date (odd-days counting across leap years) or after n days.
Clock angle between the hands at a given time (30H − 5.5M) or time when hands coincide/are opposite.
Overlapping groups described as counts in each region of a three-circle Venn diagram; find how many belong to an exact combination (e.g. both A and B but not C).
Choose the description of the Venn diagram that best represents three classes (one inside another, partial overlap, disjoint).
Linear or circular seating of 5–7 persons with 4–6 clues (immediate neighbour, 'second to the left', ends); question asks who sits at a position or between two people.
Mirror image of a clock time or of an alphanumeric/number string (vertical mirror on the right); time question solved by 11:60 − time.
A square sheet is folded once or twice and punched/cut; predict how it looks (number/position of holes) when unfolded.
Count triangles/squares in a figure built from a square or triangle with diagonals and mid-lines.
Dice: from two or three positions of the same die, find the face opposite to a given face; or a painted cube cut into n³ small cubes – count cubes with 0/1/2/3 painted faces.

Ancient and medieval India: dynasty founders, capitals, rulers' titles, Buddhist/Jain councils, Delhi Sultanate/Mughal/Vijayanagara rulers, battles with years and administrative reforms; distractors are rulers of the same or adjacent dynasty.
Modern India and freedom struggle: founders of organisations/newspapers, INC sessions and presidents, movements with years, Governors-General and their acts.
Article-number question: which Article deals with a given provision (FR, DPSP, office, emergency, finance); distractors are nearby Article numbers.
Constitution-making, Preamble, amendments, schedules and parts with their subject matter (e.g. which Schedule/amendment added X); distractors are adjacent schedules/amendments.
Constitutional/statutory offices: appointment, qualification (age), tenure, removal, oath, and borrowed features of the Constitution.
Indian physical geography: rivers (origin, tributaries, states), lakes, passes, hills, national parks and their states.
Soils, crops, minerals, climate and resources of India (which soil/crop/mineral/region; seasons and winds).
World/physical geography: atmosphere layers, ocean currents, straits, planets, latitudes and landforms.
Banking and monetary policy: RBI instruments (repo, CRR, SLR), functions, institutions and their headquarters.
Economic concepts and planning: GDP/GNP, deficits, inflation measures, Five-Year Plans, taxes, government schemes and their launch.
Physics: SI units and instruments, and everyday phenomena (mirrors/lenses, dispersion, sound speed, heat, electricity).
Chemistry: common names/formulae of compounds, ores and alloys, acids in foods, pH, gases and periodic-table facts.
Human biology: vitamins/minerals and deficiency diseases, organs and glands, blood, diseases and their causative agents.
Plant biology and classification: tissues, photosynthesis, plant hormones, cell organelles, scientists behind classification.
Performing arts and festivals: classical/folk dances, festivals and fairs with their states, instruments and their maestros.
Temples, monuments and architectural styles with their builders/dynasties and locations.
Recent national/international events of the last 1–2 years: summits and hosts, missions, schemes and major appointments.
Sports: number of players, terms and trophies of a sport, venues, and recent Olympic/Asian Games/World Cup results involving India.
Defence/CAPF static GK: raising year, headquarters, mottos and borders guarded by forces, gallantry awards, missiles and military exercises.
Unit digit of a power/product or remainder of a large power on division (cyclicity); distractors are adjacent cycle values.
Divisibility and number properties: smallest digit/number to add or subtract for divisibility by 9, 11, 8, which number is divisible, count of factors, primes, or sum of numbers in a range.
Basic/successive percentage: x% of a number, net effect of successive increases/decreases, or price rise vs consumption cut.
Percentage word problems: election votes, pass-fail marks, salary spent/saved; find the total or the difference.
Marked price above cost with a discount (or successive discounts) – find profit % or marked price.
Cost/selling price relation: profit % from CP and SP, CP from SP and gain %, CP of x items = SP of y items, two articles sold at the same price, or false-weight dealers.
Simple interest: find rate/time/principal from amounts, or the time to become n times.
Compound interest for 2–3 years, CI − SI difference, or half-yearly compounding.
Divide an amount in a given (sometimes fractional) ratio, or find shares/partnership profit.
Ratio change: number added/subtracted to change a ratio, combined ratio A : B : C, or mean/third proportional.
Mixture: add water/replace part of a mixture to reach a new ratio, or alligation of two prices/concentrations.
Average: simple or consecutive-number averages, inclusion/exclusion/replacement of a member (teacher's age, wrong entry corrected), or overlap of first-k and last-k averages.
Two/three workers with individual days; together, one leaves after some days, or efficiency ratio problems.
Pipes and cisterns (filling and emptying pipes together) or men-days (M₁D₁ = M₂D₂) proportionality.
Trains crossing a pole/platform/another train (same or opposite direction) with km/h ↔ m/s conversion.
Average speed for to-and-fro journeys, relative speed/chase problems, or boats and streams.
Reciprocal identities: given x ± 1/x = k, find x² + 1/x², x³ ± 1/x³ or x⁴ + 1/x⁴; distractors from sign slips.
Symmetric identities in a, b, c: (a + b + c)², a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc, or a + b + c = 0 shortcuts; also surds like (√a ± √b).
Triangle properties: angle at incentre/orthocentre, angle-bisector/median length, similarity ratios, Pythagorean right-triangle facts.
Circle theorems: chords intersecting, tangent length, angle in a semicircle, cyclic quadrilateral opposite angles.
Polygons and lines: interior/exterior angles, number of sides or diagonals, angles of a triangle with given ratios.
2-D mensuration: area/perimeter of rectangles, triangles (Heron's), circles and sectors, change in area with change in dimensions.
3-D mensuration: volume/surface area of cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone, sphere/hemisphere; melting and recasting.
Standard-angle values and identity simplification (sin²θ + cos²θ, complementary angles like tan 10° tan 80°).
Conditional trigonometry: given sec θ + tan θ, tan θ = a/b or similar, find another ratio/expression.
Small table/bar data (given in text) for 4–6 years or items: ratio, percentage increase, average or difference between categories.
Factual RC question on a 150–250-word passage: answer is stated in the passage; distractors use passage words with altered meaning.
Inference/main-idea/title RC question: choose the central theme or what the author implies.
Vocabulary/tone in context: synonym/antonym of a word used in the passage or the author's tone.
Cloze passage with five numbered blanks; each item tests contextual vocabulary, a connector or a preposition; distractors are near-synonyms that fail the collocation.
Single-sentence blank requiring the contextually correct word (collocation, near-synonym choice).
Single-sentence blank testing grammar – prepositions, articles, tense, conjunctions.
Synonym of a standalone or underlined word (moderate CGL-level vocabulary); distractors include antonyms and look-alike words.
Antonym of a standalone or underlined word; the trap option is a synonym of the given word.
Meaning of a common idiom/phrase (or the idiom that fits a sentence); distractors are literal readings.
One-word substitute for a descriptive phrase (persons, -cide, -phobia, -archy words); distractors are related words of the same family.
Select the correctly (or incorrectly) spelt word among four look-alike spellings (double letters, ie/ei, -ance/-ence).
Sentence split into 3–4 segments; error in subject–verb agreement, pronoun or noun number (each/one of/neither…nor, uncountable nouns).
Sentence split into segments; error in tense sequence, preposition, comparative/superlative, or conjunction pairs (hardly…when, no sooner…than).
Improve the bracketed/underlined part: tense, conditional, preposition or idiom usage; 'No improvement' sometimes an option.
Change active to passive (or vice versa) across tenses, including questions and modals; distractors change the tense.
Direct ↔ indirect speech: reporting verb change, backshift of tense, pronoun and time-word changes; imperatives with 'ordered/requested'.

resources.notes: SSC publishes tentative answer keys with candidates' response sheets (question papers) on ssc.gov.in for a short window after Paper 1 and Paper 2; final keys after results. No permanent official PYQ archive; memory-based papers are compiled by coaching sites.

questions.question:
Select the letter-cluster that is related to the third cluster in the same way as the second is related to the first.
ACE : FHJ :: MOQ : ?
questions.explanation: Each letter moves 5 places forward: A→F, C→H, E→J. So M→R, O→T, Q→V.

questions.question: Select the letter-pair that does not belong to the group.
questions.explanation: In BD, FH and JL there is a gap of one letter (+2). In NQ the gap is two letters (+3).

relevance.note: Odd letter-pair by +3 gap; CPO classification

questions.question:
Select the number that will come next in the series.
6, 11, 21, 36, 56, ?
questions.explanation: Differences: 5, 10, 15, 20, so next is 25: 56 + 25 = 81.

questions.question:
Select the number that will come next in the series.
0, 6, 24, 60, 120, ?

relevance.note: n³−n series with 216 cube trap; CPO

questions.question: 'A + B' means A is the mother of B; 'A − B' means A is the brother of B; 'A × B' means A is the father of B. What does 'P × Q − R' mean?
options: P is the uncle of R
P is the brother of R
P is the father of R
P is the grandfather of R
questions.explanation: P × Q: P is the father of Q. Q − R: Q is the brother of R, so R is also P's child. Hence P is the father of R.

relevance.note: Coded blood relation with brother/uncle trap; CPO

questions.question: A man walks 30 m towards South, turns left and walks 40 m, then turns left again and walks 30 m. How far and in which direction is he from his starting point?
questions.explanation: South 30 → (0, −30); left of South is East: 40 → (40, −30); left of East is North: 30 → (40, 0). He is 40 m East of the start.

relevance.note: Three-leg U walk net 40 m East; CPO direction

questions.question:
Statements:
All teachers are graduates.
Some graduates are engineers.
Conclusions:
I. Some teachers are engineers.
II. All engineers are graduates.
Which conclusion(s) follow(s)?
questions.explanation: The engineers who are graduates need not be teachers, so I is not certain. 'Some graduates are engineers' does not make all engineers graduates, so II does not follow.

questions.question:
If '÷' means '+', '×' means '−', '+' means '×' and '−' means '÷', what is the value of:
12 + 3 ÷ 40 − 8 × 6
If 2 * 3 = 13 and 3 * 4 = 25, then what is 4 * 5?

Arrange the following words in the order in which they appear in an English dictionary.
1. Gather  2. Garden  3. Gallop  4. Gamble  5. Gaze
questions.explanation: Compare the third letters: Ga-l, Ga-m, Ga-r, Ga-t, Ga-z → Gallop, Gamble, Garden, Gather, Gaze = 3, 4, 2, 1, 5.

questions.question: 26 January 1950, the day the Constitution of India came into force, fell on which day of the week?
questions.explanation: Odd-day method: 1600 years → 0 odd days; 300 years → 1; 49 years (12 leap + 37 ordinary) → 12×2 + 37 = 61 → 5 odd days; 26 days of January → 5. Total = 11 → 4 odd days = Thursday.

relevance.note: 26 Jan 1950 was a Thursday; odd-day calendar item seen in SSC

questions.question: Who was the first woman President of the Indian National Congress?
questions.explanation: Annie Besant presided over the Calcutta session of 1917. Sarojini Naidu (Kanpur, 1925) was the first Indian woman President.

relevance.note: First woman INC president Annie Besant with Naidu trap; CPO

questions.question: Who among the following is regarded as the founder of the Ghadar Party (1913)?
questions.explanation: The Ghadar Party was founded in 1913 on the Pacific coast of the USA by Lala Har Dayal along with Sohan Singh Bhakna and others.

relevance.note: Ghadar Party–Har Dayal; CPO modern history

questions.question: The Permanent Settlement of land revenue in Bengal (1793) was introduced by which Governor-General?
questions.explanation: Lord Cornwallis introduced the Permanent Settlement (Zamindari system) in 1793.

questions.question: Which Article of the Constitution of India provides for the office of the Attorney General of India?
questions.explanation: Article 76 – Attorney General; 148 – CAG; 165 – Advocate General of a State; 124 – Supreme Court.

relevance.note: Article 76 Attorney General with CAG/Advocate General traps; CPO

questions.question: Which Constitutional Amendment Act gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj institutions?
questions.explanation: The 73rd Amendment added Part IX (Panchayats) and the Eleventh Schedule; the 74th did the same for municipalities.

relevance.note: 73rd Amendment Panchayati Raj with 74th trap; CPO

questions.question: Which mountain pass connects Srinagar with Leh?
questions.explanation: Zoji La lies on the Srinagar–Leh highway. Nathu La is in Sikkim, Shipki La in Himachal Pradesh, Bomdi La in Arunachal Pradesh.

questions.question: Which is the largest freshwater lake in India?
questions.explanation: Wular Lake in Jammu & Kashmir is the largest freshwater lake; Chilika is a brackish-water lagoon.

relevance.note: Wular largest freshwater lake with Chilika trap; CPO

questions.question: The Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) was originally raised in 1939 under which name?
questions.explanation: CRPF was raised on 27 July 1939 as the Crown Representative's Police and renamed CRPF by an Act of Parliament in 1949.

relevance.note: CRPF raised as Crown Representative's Police; CPO defence static

questions.question: What is the remainder when 2³¹ is divided by 5?
questions.explanation: Powers of 2 mod 5 cycle as 2, 4, 3, 1. 31 = 4 × 7 + 3, so the remainder is the 3rd term = 3.

questions.question: In an election between two candidates, the winner got 58% of the valid votes and won by 2,880 votes. What was the total number of valid votes?
questions.explanation: Margin = 58% − 42% = 16% of valid votes = 2880 → total = 18,000.

questions.question: A dishonest shopkeeper claims to sell rice at cost price but uses a weight of 900 g instead of 1 kg. What is his gain percentage?
questions.explanation: Gain % = (error/true weight given) × 100 = 100/900 × 100 = 11 1/9 %.

relevance.note: False weight 900 g gain 11 1/9% with 10% trap; CPO

questions.question: A 60-litre mixture contains milk and water in the ratio 2 : 1. How much water must be added to make the ratio 1 : 2?
questions.explanation: Milk = 40 L, water = 20 L. For 1 : 2, water must be 80 L, so add 60 L.

relevance.note: Water to reverse 2:1 ratio; CPO mixture

questions.question: Two trains of lengths 150 m and 100 m are running in opposite directions at 50 km/h and 40 km/h. In how much time will they cross each other?
questions.explanation: Relative speed = 90 km/h = 25 m/s. Time = (150 + 100)/25 = 10 s.

questions.question: If x = √3 + √2, what is the value of x + 1/x?
In a right-angled triangle, the two sides containing the right angle are 9 cm and 12 cm. What is the length of the median drawn to the hypotenuse?
questions.explanation: Hypotenuse = √(81 + 144) = 15 cm. The median to the hypotenuse is half of it = 7.5 cm.

relevance.note: Median to hypotenuse half; CPO geometry

questions.question: What is the total surface area of a closed cylinder of radius 7 cm and height 10 cm? (Take π = 22/7)
If tan θ = 3/4 and θ is acute, what is the value of (sin θ + cos θ)/(sin θ − cos θ)?

Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
METICULOUS
questions.explanation: Meticulous means showing great attention to detail – painstaking.

questions.question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.
BENEVOLENT
questions.explanation: Benevolent (well-meaning, kind) is opposite to malevolent (wishing harm).

relevance.note: BENEVOLENT antonym Malevolent with synonym traps; CPO

questions.question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the idiom.
To bite the bullet
options: To be injured in a fight
To face a difficult situation with courage
questions.explanation: 'Bite the bullet' means to make oneself do something unpleasant or difficult bravely.

questions.question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the idiom.
To be on the horns of a dilemma
options: To be in a very aggressive mood
To face a choice between two equally unpleasant options
questions.explanation: Being on the horns of a dilemma means having to choose between two equally undesirable alternatives.

relevance.note: Horns of a dilemma; CPO idiom

questions.question:
Select the one-word substitute for the given phrase.
The killing of one's own brother
questions.explanation: Fratricide = killing a brother; patricide = father; regicide = king; genocide = a whole people.

questions.question: Select the correctly spelt word.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is 'lieutenant'.

questions.question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error, or 'No error'.
The police / has arrested / the culprit.
questions.explanation: 'Police' is a plural noun, so it takes a plural verb: The police have arrested the culprit.

questions.question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error, or 'No error'.
No sooner did / the bell ring / when the students rushed out.
questions.explanation: 'No sooner' is followed by 'than', not 'when': No sooner did the bell ring than the students rushed out.

questions.question:
Select the most appropriate option to improve the bracketed part of the sentence.
He [insisted to go] there alone.
questions.explanation: 'Insist' takes the preposition 'on' followed by a gerund: insisted on going.

questions.question:
Select the passive form of the given sentence.
They will complete the project by Friday.
options: The project would be completed by them by Friday.
The project will have been completed by them by Friday.
The project is completed by them by Friday.
The project will be completed by them by Friday.
questions.explanation: Simple future active (will complete) becomes 'will be completed' in the passive.

relevance.note: Future passive with future-perfect trap; CPO

questions.question:
Select the correct indirect form of the given sentence.
The officer said to the constable, "Close the gate at once."
options: The officer said to the constable that close the gate at once.
The officer ordered the constable that he closes the gate at once.
The officer ordered the constable to close the gate at once.
The officer ordered the constable to have closed the gate at once.
questions.explanation: An imperative (command) is reported with 'ordered + object + to-infinitive': ordered the constable to close the gate at once.

questions.question:
Select the option that is related to the third number in the same way as the second number is related to the first number and the sixth number is related to the fifth number.
(NOTE: Operations should be performed on the whole numbers, without breaking down the numbers into their constituent digits.)
12 : 150 :: 9 : ? :: 15 : 231

relevance.note: n²+6 triple analogy with NOTE; exact SSC format

questions.question:
Select the option that is related to the third word in the same way as the second word is related to the first word.
Odometer : Distance :: Hygrometer : ?
questions.explanation: An odometer measures distance travelled; a hygrometer measures humidity.

questions.question:
Select the option that is related to the third letter-cluster in the same way as the second letter-cluster is related to the first letter-cluster.
PLAN : RNCP :: SHOT : ?
questions.explanation: Each letter moves +2: P→R, L→N, A→C, N→P. So S→U, H→J, O→Q, T→V.

questions.question:
Three of the following four number-pairs are alike in a certain way and one is different. Select the odd number-pair.
(NOTE: Operations should be performed on the whole numbers, without breaking down the numbers into their constituent digits.)
questions.explanation: In the others the second number is the cube of the first. 6³ = 216, not 206.

relevance.note: Number-pair cube rule with NOTE; CPO

questions.question:
Select the letter-cluster that will come next in the following series.
DKP, FMR, HOT, JQV, ?
questions.explanation: Each letter moves +2: J→L, Q→S, V→X.

questions.question: In a certain code language, 'BRAVE' is written as 'FWBSC'. How will 'SHIELD' be written in that language?
questions.explanation: The word is reversed and each letter moved +1: BRAVE → EVARB → FWBSC. SHIELD → DLEIHS → EMFJIT.

relevance.note: Reverse +1 coding with six letters; CPO

questions.question: In a certain code language, 'GOLD' is coded as 70 and 'IRON' is coded as 52. How will 'STEEL' be coded in that language?
questions.explanation: Code = sum of reverse alphabet positions (A = 26 … Z = 1). GOLD: 20 + 12 + 15 + 23 = 70; IRON: 18 + 9 + 12 + 13 = 52; STEEL: 8 + 7 + 22 + 22 + 15 = 74. (61 is the forward sum.)

relevance.note: Reverse-position sum coding; CPO hard coding

questions.question:
Which two mathematical signs should be interchanged to make the given equation correct?
42 × 6 + 8 ÷ 3 − 11 = 20
questions.explanation: Interchanging × and ÷ gives 42 ÷ 6 + 8 × 3 − 11 = 7 + 24 − 11 = 20. The other swaps do not give 20.

questions.question: If 5 # 3 = 49, 7 # 2 = 67 and 4 # 6 = 76, then what is the value of 8 # 3?

relevance.note: a²+b²+ab defined operation from three examples; CPO

questions.question:
In a certain code language, 'A # B' means 'A is the brother of B', 'A @ B' means 'A is the mother of B', 'A & B' means 'A is the husband of B' and 'A % B' means 'A is the son of B'.
If P & Q @ R # S, how is P related to S?
questions.explanation: P is the husband of Q, Q is the mother of R, and R is the brother of S, so S is also Q's child. P, Q's husband, is S's father.

questions.question:
Which of the following words will come third if they are arranged in the order in which they appear in an English dictionary?
Marine, Mariner, Margin, Marigold, Maritime
questions.explanation: Order: Margin, Marigold, Marine, Mariner, Maritime. The third word is Marine.

relevance.note: Third word in Mar- dictionary order; CPO

questions.question: Who composed the Prayag Prashasti (Allahabad Pillar inscription) in praise of Samudragupta?
questions.explanation: Harisena, Samudragupta's court poet, composed it. Ravikirti wrote the Aihole inscription of Pulakeshin II; Banabhatta was Harsha's court poet.

questions.question: Who founded the Indian Association in Calcutta in 1876 along with Ananda Mohan Bose?
questions.explanation: The Indian Association was founded by Surendranath Banerjee and Ananda Mohan Bose in 1876.

questions.question: Which Governor-General abolished the practice of Sati in 1829?
questions.explanation: Bengal Sati Regulation XVII of 1829 was passed under Lord William Bentinck.

questions.question: Under which Article of the Constitution of India can the President proclaim a National Emergency?
questions.explanation: Article 352 – National Emergency; 356 – President's Rule in a state; 360 – Financial Emergency.

relevance.note: Article 352 national emergency with 356/360 traps; CPO

questions.question: Which Schedule of the Constitution of India contains the Union List, the State List and the Concurrent List?
questions.explanation: The Seventh Schedule distributes legislative subjects between the Union and the States.

questions.question: The Nathu La pass, located in Sikkim, connects India with which region?
questions.explanation: Nathu La on the Dongkya range links Sikkim with the Tibet Autonomous Region of China.

questions.question: In government budgeting, 'fiscal deficit' refers to:
options: Total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings
Value of imports minus value of exports
questions.explanation: Fiscal deficit = total expenditure − (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts), i.e. the government's borrowing requirement. The other options define revenue deficit, primary deficit and trade deficit.

relevance.note: Fiscal deficit definition with revenue/primary traps; CPO

questions.question: The Brihadeeswarar Temple at Thanjavur was built by which ruler?
questions.explanation: Rajaraja Chola I completed the temple around 1010 CE; it is part of the 'Great Living Chola Temples' World Heritage Site.

relevance.note: Brihadeeswarar–Rajaraja I with Rajendra trap; CPO

questions.question: Which force is popularly known as the 'Black Cats'?
questions.explanation: The NSG commandos are known as 'Black Cats' because of their black uniforms.

questions.question: What is the remainder when 3⁴⁵ is divided by 8?
What is the least number which, when divided by 6, 9 and 15, leaves a remainder of 4 in each case?
questions.explanation: LCM of 6, 9, 15 = 90, so the least such number is 90 + 4 = 94.

questions.question: The population of a town increases by 10% in the first year and decreases by 10% in the second year. If the present population is 50,000, what will it be after two years?
A shopkeeper sells two watches for ₹4,800 each. On one he gains 20% and on the other he loses 20%. What is his overall gain or loss?

relevance.note: Same SP ±20% loss in rupees; CPO

questions.question: The difference between the compound interest (compounded annually) and the simple interest on a sum for 2 years at 8% per annum is ₹96. What is the sum?
Two numbers are in the ratio 4 : 7. If 6 is added to each number, the ratio becomes 2 : 3. What is the larger number?
In what ratio must rice costing ₹42 per kg be mixed with rice costing ₹54 per kg so that the mixture costs ₹50 per kg?

relevance.note: Alligation of rice prices with reversed-ratio trap; CPO

questions.question: A is twice as efficient as B. Working together, they finish a piece of work in 14 days. In how many days can A alone finish the work?
questions.explanation: Efficiencies 2 : 1; total work = 3 × 14 = 42 units. A alone: 42/2 = 21 days.

questions.question: A boat covers 30 km downstream in 2 hours and the same distance upstream in 3 hours. What is the speed of the stream?
questions.explanation: Downstream speed = 15 km/h, upstream = 10 km/h. Stream speed = (15 − 10)/2 = 2.5 km/h.

relevance.note: Stream speed from down/up times; CPO

questions.question: If x + 1/x = 2√3, what is the value of x³ + 1/x³?
ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral in which ∠A = (2x + 10)° and ∠C = (3x + 20)°. What is the measure of ∠A?
questions.explanation: Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary: 5x + 30 = 180, x = 30. ∠A = 70°.

questions.question: The sides of a triangle are 13 cm, 14 cm and 15 cm. What is its area?
What is the value of sin² 25° + sin² 65° + tan 30° × tan 60°?
questions.explanation: sin² 65° = cos² 25°, so the first two terms sum to 1; tan 30° × tan 60° = 1. Total = 2.

questions.question: The annual expenditure (in ₹ thousand) of a family is: Food – 96, Rent – 72, Education – 48, Travel – 24, Others – 60. What percentage of the total expenditure is spent on Education?
questions.explanation: Total = 300. Education = 48/300 × 100 = 16%.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Digital payments have made life remarkably convenient, but they have also opened the door to a new kind of crime. Fraudsters no longer need to break into a house; a single phone call or a cleverly worded message is often enough. Posing as bank officials, delivery agents or even police officers, they create a sense of urgency and persuade victims to share one-time passwords or to click on harmful links. Older citizens and first-time internet users are particularly vulnerable, but educated professionals are by no means immune. Experts insist that awareness is the strongest defence. Banks never ask customers to reveal their passwords, and genuine officials do not demand immediate payment over the phone. Victims are advised to report fraud at once on the national cyber-crime helpline 1930, because money can often be frozen if the complaint reaches the bank within the first few hours.

According to the passage, how do fraudsters usually persuade their victims?
options: By breaking into their houses at night
By posing as trusted officials and creating a sense of urgency
By offering them jobs in banks
By sending them free mobile phones
questions.explanation: The passage says they pose as bank officials, delivery agents or police and create a sense of urgency.

Select the most appropriate synonym of the word 'immune' as used in the passage.

questions.question:
Read the passage and select the most appropriate option for the numbered blank.

A good police officer must be both firm and fair. Citizens are more likely to (1) ______ the law when they believe it is applied equally to all. An officer who loses his temper or shows (2) ______ towards one group quickly loses the public's respect. Patience, (3) ______, is as important as physical strength. Officers who listen carefully to complaints often (4) ______ disputes before they turn violent, and in doing so they (5) ______ the trust on which effective policing depends.

Select the most appropriate option for blank (2).
questions.explanation: Showing unfair preference (favouritism) towards one group would lose public respect; the other qualities would not.

questions.question:
Read the passage and select the most appropriate option for the numbered blank.

A good police officer must be both firm and fair. Citizens are more likely to (1) ______ the law when they believe it is applied equally to all. An officer who loses his temper or shows (2) ______ towards one group quickly loses the public's respect. Patience, (3) ______, is as important as physical strength. Officers who listen carefully to complaints often (4) ______ disputes before they turn violent, and in doing so they (5) ______ the trust on which effective policing depends.

Select the most appropriate option for blank (4).
questions.explanation: Officers who listen carefully settle (resolve) disputes before they turn violent.

questions.question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
CANDOUR
questions.explanation: Candour is the quality of being open and honest – frankness. Deceit is its opposite.

questions.question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.
OBSCURE
questions.explanation: Obscure means unclear or hidden; its antonym is evident. The other options are synonyms.

relevance.note: OBSCURE antonym with synonym traps; CPO

questions.question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
Government in which power rests with a small group of people
questions.explanation: Oligarchy is rule by a few; monarchy by one ruler, democracy by the people, anarchy is the absence of government.

questions.question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error, or 'No error'.
Mathematics are / my favourite subject / at school
questions.explanation: 'Mathematics' is singular in meaning, so it takes 'is': 'Mathematics is my favourite subject.'

questions.question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error, or 'No error'.
Of the two candidates, / Ramesh is / the best suited for the post
options: the best suited for the post
questions.explanation: When two people are compared, the comparative is used: 'the better suited', not 'the best suited'.

relevance.note: Of the two … best → better; CPO comparative

questions.question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the bracketed part of the sentence.
Unless you [do not work] hard, you will not pass the examination.
questions.explanation: 'Unless' already means 'if not', so another 'not' is wrong: 'Unless you work hard…'.

relevance.note: Unless … do not double negative; CPO

questions.question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.
The thief was being chased by the constable.
options: The constable has been chasing the thief.
The constable was chasing the thief.
The constable is chasing the thief.
questions.explanation: 'Was being + V3' is past continuous passive; the active form is 'was chasing'.

questions.question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in indirect speech.
The inspector said to the guard, "Do not let anyone enter the room."
options: The inspector ordered the guard that do not let anyone enter the room.
The inspector told the guard not to let anyone entered the room.
The inspector said to the guard to not let anyone enter the room.
The inspector ordered the guard not to let anyone enter the room.
questions.explanation: A negative command is reported with 'ordered/told + object + not to + base verb'.

relevance.note: Negative imperative → ordered not to; CPO

questions.question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
The suspect gave an ______ account of his whereabouts, which made the police doubt his story.
questions.explanation: An inconsistent account (one that contradicts itself) would make the police doubt the story.
